Story supplies the type (two lexical tones on the tonic syllable; stress weak and coincident with the tonic/stem syllable) and the domain (tone group, last word). Nothing in the catalog is contradicted since nothing was recorded.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tlingit (central dialect) has two lexical tones, high and low, contrastive only on the tonic syllable of the tone group (a unit of one or more grammatical words). Stress is weak ('syllables are little differentiated by stress') and falls on the tonic syllable, which is always a stem syllable and sits in the last word of the tone group; relative to the tone group it may be final, penultimate or antepenultimate (the latter two when suffixes/clitics follow the stem). So word stress is effectively root/stem-anchored and the tone-bearing syllable is the stressed one; it is not counted from an edge of the word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such. In tone patterns 5 and 6 (low-tone tonic on the penult or antepenult of the tone group) the syllable immediately after the tonic, if it has a long vowel, 'may be equally stressed with the tonic syllable' (p. 15). The precontour (pre-tonic syllables) is low-mid in pitch; its first syllable and closed/long-vowel syllables are slightly higher (p. 15).
new_statements.exceptions: Tone group extensions (syllabic clitics) are never tonic (p. 15-16). Laryngeals occur only as onsets of tonic syllables (p. 9, 13). Low tone does not occur with short vowels (p. 14). Story notes dialect differences in 'intonational features' (p. 2) and describes the central dialect only.
new_statements.identity_note: Story 1966 describes the central dialect of Tlingit (fieldwork 1959-1963 at Angoon, Admiralty Island, SE Alaska, with short visits to Hoonah, Juneau, Kake, Klukwan, Sitka, Carcross, Teslin); she notes dialects differ partly in 'intonational features' (p. 2). Buschmann 1857 treats 'die Sprache der Koloschen' (= Tlingit) from 18th-19th c. wordlists (Veniaminov's Sitka-area material, Lisiansky, Marchand/Chanal/Roblet, Wrangell, Davydov), not from fieldwork.

sources.note: Northern Tlingit has two contrastive tones, high and low, on short and long vowels, length orthogonal to tone (4 qualities x 4 = 16 vowel phonemes, plus idiolectally 'variable length' vowels in suffixes/enclitics). Some noun suffixes (possessive -i, locative-predicate -u, -tee 'all', etc.) show ALTERNATING tone - high after a low-tone stem, low after a high-tone stem - while others (e.g. -dáx̱, -náx̱) have fixed tone regardless of the stem. OT analysis: alternating tone = OCP(T) acting on TBUs lexically unspecified for tone (inserted tone obeys the OCP), fixed tone = lexically specified tone…

sources.note: Tlingit tracks prominence-by-tone and prominence-by-weight; a combination of tone and weight identifies the stem as prominent (additive calculus of prominence), and the graded distribution of proclitics, prefixes, suffixes and enclitics relative to tone and weight follows prosodic structure isomorphic with syntax — i.e. a full treatment of how lexical/stem tone and syllable weight interact across the Tlingit word.

tone.says: ANLA record: phonology of the (toneless) Tongass dialect and its significance, with discussion of Saanyaa, Heinyaa, Southern and Northern Tlingit — the source description of the vowel stigmata (fading, glottalized, long) that correspond to low/high(/falling) tone in the tonal dialects; cited as the basis of Hamp 1979 and Crippen 2012.
